transfer_rules.rule_name: No legal limit on carrying currency in or out
transfer_rules.rule_summary: You can legally bring any amount of cash or monetary instruments into or out of the US. Amounts over USD 10,000 must be reported (see FinCEN Form 105).
transfer_rules.restrictions: Amounts over USD 10,000 (or foreign equivalent) at one time must be reported to CBP on FinCEN Form 105.
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: It is legal to transport any amount of currency or other monetary instruments into or out of the United States.

transfer_rules.rule_name: Report cash over USD 10,000 crossing the border (FinCEN Form 105)
transfer_rules.rule_summary: If you physically carry, mail or ship more than USD 10,000 (or the foreign equivalent) in cash or monetary instruments into or out of the US at one time, you must report it on FinCEN Form 105. This covers physical money, not bank wires.
documents_required: FinCEN Form 105 (Report of International Transportation of Currency or Monetary Instruments)
transfer_rules.restrictions: Threshold is an aggregate amount exceeding USD 10,000 at one time. The duty also falls on a person in the US who receives such a shipment from abroad when no report was filed.
transfer_rules.regulator: Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), U.S. Department of the Treasury; collected by U.S. Customs and Border Protection
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: an aggregate amount exceeding $10,000 at one time

transfer_rules.rule_name: Banks report cash transactions over USD 10,000 (CTR)
transfer_rules.rule_summary: US banks must file a Currency Transaction Report when you deposit or withdraw more than USD 10,000 in cash (coins and notes) in one business day. The bank files it, not you. Splitting cash into smaller amounts to avoid a report is a crime.
documents_required: Government-issued ID and personal information requested by the bank
transfer_rules.restrictions: Multiple cash transactions by or for the same person in one business day are added together. Breaking up transactions to avoid reporting (structuring) is a federal crime.
transfer_rules.exceptions: Applies to currency (cash or coin) transactions. Wire transfers are a separate regime.
transfer_rules.regulator: Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), U.S. Department of the Treasury
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: Federal law requires financial institutions to report currency (cash or coin) transactions over $10,000.

transfer_rules.rule_name: Funds-transfer 'travel rule' for transfers of USD 3,000+
transfer_rules.rule_summary: For wire transfers of USD 3,000 or more (or the foreign equivalent), the sending bank must include your name, address and account number, plus the transfer details and recipient information, with the payment.
documents_required: Recipient name, address and account number (if received)
transfer_rules.restrictions: Applies to transmittals of funds equal to or greater than USD 3,000. The fetched page did not state a separate recordkeeping threshold.
transfer_rules.regulator: Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), U.S. Department of the Treasury
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: Only transmittals of funds equal to or greater than $3,000 (or its foreign equivalent) are subject to this rule

transfer_rules.residency_condition: All U.S. persons, and all individuals and entities within the United States
transfer_rules.rule_name: OFAC sanctions screening applies to all transfers
transfer_rules.rule_summary: US sanctions rules apply to everyone in the US, including international students. Banks screen transfers and can block or reject payments involving sanctioned countries, people or entities, whatever the amount.
transfer_rules.restrictions: Transactions involving sanctioned jurisdictions, regimes or persons may be blocked or rejected.
transfer_rules.exceptions: Non-U.S. persons are also subject to certain prohibitions (for example, causing a U.S. person to violate sanctions).
transfer_rules.regulator: Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), U.S. Department of the Treasury
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: All U.S. persons must comply with OFAC sanctions

transfer_rules.rule_summary: When you send more than USD 15 electronically from the US to another country, the provider must show fees, taxes, exchange rate and the amount that will arrive before and after you pay. You can cancel free within 30 minutes and have 180 days to report an error.
transfer_rules.restrictions: Covers electronic transfers of more than USD 15 sent by consumers in the United States to people or companies in foreign countries. Error notice within 180 days of the date funds were to be available.
transfer_rules.exceptions: The 30-minute cancellation window ends early if the recipient has already picked up the funds or they have been deposited. Does not cover money sent into the US.
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: you have up to 30 minutes to cancel the remittance transfer at no charge

transfer_rules.residency_condition: U.S. persons only (citizens, residents, and U.S. entities, trusts and estates)
transfer_rules.rule_name: FBAR: U.S. persons with foreign accounts over USD 10,000
transfer_rules.rule_summary: U.S. persons whose foreign bank and financial accounts together exceeded USD 10,000 at any time in a year must file an FBAR (FinCEN Form 114) electronically, due April 15 of the following year. Check with a tax adviser whether you count as a U.S. person.
transfer_rules.restrictions: Threshold is the aggregate value of all foreign financial accounts exceeding USD 10,000 at any time during the calendar year.
transfer_rules.exceptions: Applies only to U.S. persons. Whether a particular F-1 student counts as a 'resident' was not confirmed on the fetched page.
transfer_rules.regulator: Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), U.S. Department of the Treasury; information page by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS)
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: exceeded $10,000 at any time during the calendar year reported

transfer_rules.rule_name: Proof of funds for the Form I-20 and student visa
transfer_rules.rule_summary: Before your school issues a Form I-20, you must show that you or a sponsor can pay tuition, books, living costs and travel. Bring the same evidence to your visa interview and keep it with you when you enter the US.
transfer_rules.restrictions: Schools may set their own extra requirements; check with the school's international student office.
transfer_rules.exceptions: The list of example documents is not exhaustive.
transfer_rules.regulator: Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP), U.S. Department of Homeland Security
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: Designated school officials (DSOs) must collect evidence of the student's financial ability before issuing a Form I-20.

transfer_rules.rule_name: Bank ID rules for non-U.S. customers (Customer Identification Program)
transfer_rules.rule_summary: Before opening an account, a US bank must collect your name, date of birth, address and an ID number. Non-U.S. persons can give a tax ID number, or a passport number and issuing country, or another government ID number.
documents_required: Identification number: TIN (e.g. ITIN), or passport number and country of issuance, or alien ID card number, or other government-issued ID
transfer_rules.restrictions: Each bank sets its own accepted documents within these minimums.
transfer_rules.regulator: Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and other federal banking agencies, with FinCEN
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: For a non-U.S. person, one or more of the following is required: a TIN; passport number and country of issuance, alien identification card number;

account_opening.summary: An international student can usually open a US bank account without a Social Security number. By law, banks must collect your name, date of birth, address and an ID number, and non-U.S. persons may use an ITIN or a passport number and issuing country. Each bank sets its own rules. Without an SSN or ITIN you may only get an account that pays no interest. International students usually have to open the account in person at a branch.
typical_documents: Passport (foreign passports accepted by some banks)
Secondary ID such as a student photo ID or Form I-20 (e.g. Chase lists the Student I-20 as a secondary ID)
Proof of U.S. physical address (e.g. a bill, lease or letter with your name and address)
Tax ID if you have one: SSN or ITIN (some banks also accept a foreign tax ID)
Letter confirming university enrollment (requested by some banks)
eligibility_factors: SSN not always required; ITIN or passport number may be used for identity
Without an SSN or ITIN you may be limited to a no-interest account
Many banks require international or non-permanent-resident customers to open in person at a branch
A U.S. physical address is commonly required (P.O. boxes not accepted at Wells Fargo)
Some online applications require U.S. citizenship or permanent/resident-alien status (e.g. Capital One 360, Citi online)
Minimum age is typically 17 or 18 depending on bank and channel

banks.account_type: Bank of America Advantage SafeBalance Banking (Advantage Banking family)
banks.visa_requirements: Foreign passport accepted with or without a U.S.-issued visa

Tax Identification Number, if applicable (SSN, ITIN or Foreign Tax ID)
Proof of U.S. address and enrollment letter (per BofA Better Money Habits guide)
banks.minimum_balance: Opening deposit not stated on fetched pages. A USD 500 minimum daily balance is one fee-waiver option.
banks.monthly_fee: USD 4.95 for SafeBalance; waived if an owner is under 25 or with a USD 500+ minimum daily balance
banks.evidence_quote: Foreign passport with or without U.S. issued visa

Fee data from https://info.bankofamerica.com/en/student-banking/banking-accounts. banks.monthly_fee: USD 4.95, or USD 0 if the owner is age 17 through 24 or has USD 250+ in qualifying electronic deposits each statement period
banks.credit_card_available: Chase says that with an SSN or ITIN you 'should be able to apply for most credit cards'; secured cards are described as an option. Chase-specific ITIN acceptance not confirmed.

Chase's education page says non-U.S. residents 'may be able to open a bank account at some financial institutions without having an SSN'. Minimum age of 17 is the lowest age the offer page mentions. Credit card info: https://www.chase.com/personal/credit-cards/education/basics/can-international-students-get-credit-cards

documents: SSN or ITIN, OR (for non-U.S. citizens without a U.S. taxpayer ID) a government-issued ID evidencing nationality or residence, such as a passport
Two forms of ID (primary and secondary) for branch openings
Proof of physical U.S. address if not shown on ID (no P.O. Box or private mailbox)
banks.minimum_balance: Opening deposit not stated on fetched page. A USD 1,500 minimum daily balance is one fee-waiver option.
banks.monthly_fee: USD 15, waived if the primary owner is 17-24 years old (until age 25), or with USD 500+ qualifying electronic deposits, USD 1,500 minimum daily balance, or USD 5,000+ in qualifying balances

banks.notes: Non-permanent U.S. residents must make a branch appointment; online opening requires an SSN/ITIN, a physical U.S. address and age 18+. International wires go to 200+ countries; USD 30 digital / USD 40 branch wire fee; online wires need a current U.S. residence; exchange-rate markup applies. A 'Student and Teen Checking' page exists but was not fetched. Sources: https://www.wellsfargo.com/checking/everyday/ and https://www.wellsfargo.com/mobile-online-banking/wires/

banks.notes: The residency and age rule above applies to online applications. Whether international (F-1) students can open in a branch with a passport was not confirmed. Fees, opening deposit and student options were not shown on fetched pages (https://www.citi.com/banking/checking-account rendered no content). Citi says an international wire 'may be sent in USD or in the local foreign currency'.

banks.minimum_balance: No minimum deposit to open and no minimum balance to maintain
banks.evidence_quote: 360 Checking is available to United States citizens or lawful permanent residents with a U.S. physical address located in one of the 50 United States or Washington, D.C.

Outgoing international wires can only be sent through branch locations and not all account types are eligible (https://www.capitalone.com/help-center/checking-savings/wire-transfer-support/). Domestic outgoing wire: USD 30. Capital One's international-student credit card article does not confirm Capital One accepts ITINs.

what_contributes: Payment history: about 35% of a FICO Score
Amounts owed / how much of your available credit you use: about 30%
Length of credit history / age of accounts: about 15%
Credit mix (number and types of accounts): about 10%
Collections, foreclosures or bankruptcies, and how long ago they happened
why_it_matters: Lenders use it to decide whether to offer mortgages, credit cards and auto loans
It affects the interest rates and credit limits you are offered
Used for tenant screening when renting
Rental payment history can appear in credit reports, and landlords use specialty tenant-screening reports
responsible_behaviours: Pay every bill on time; set up automatic payments or reminders
If you missed payments, get current and stay current
Keep balances low compared with your credit limit
Apply only for the credit you need; avoid many applications in a short period
Check your credit reports and dispute errors; get one free report from each bureau every 12 months
Ask your landlord whether they report rent payments, since on-time rent can help build credit
risks: Late or missed payments lower your score and stay on your report
High balances relative to your limits hurt your score
Many credit applications in a short period can signal financial trouble to lenders
Late rent and debts sent to collection can appear in credit reports
A landlord can deny you based on a tenant-screening report; you are entitled to an adverse action notice
credit_system.foreigner_notes: Credit history from other countries does not transfer to the US credit system, so newcomers usually start with no US score. Some lenders may consider international credit history in limited cases. Common ways to start are a secured credit card (refundable deposit, often from about USD 200), being added as an authorized user on someone's card, or a credit-builder loan. Some card issuers accept an ITIN instead of an SSN; check each issuer.
